newsitem.title: GERMANY: Rise in German unemployment slows in February.
newsitem.headline: Rise in German unemployment slows in February.

text.p: German unemployment worsened again in February but the rise in joblessness slowed, the Federal Labour Office said Thursday, prompting analysts to predict the worst of the jobs crisis may be over.

Still, unemployment remains at the highest levels since the Great Depression of the 1930s, undermining Germany's efforts to cut its budget deficit and eroding what leverage it has to exclude supposedly weaker nations from European monetary union, slated to start in January 1999, economists said.

Unemployment rose a mere 5,000 to a seasonally adjusted 4.316 million in February, the Federal Labour Office said. The Bundesbank said the unemployment rate was unchanged from January at 11.3 percent.
The unadjusted total number of unemployed was 4.672 million, up from 4.658 million in January. The unadjusted rate was also unchanged at 12.2 percent.

In January, a sharp rise of 145,000 in the seasonally adjusted total fuelled speculation Germany would fail to narrow its budget gap this year and miss the deficit target for the single European currency.

Labour Office President Bernhard Jagoda told a news conference the worst of Germany's jobs crisis may now be over since the rise in unemployment slowed sharply in February. He added he expected a decline in unemployment in March.

"In non-construction related manufacturing areas, the rise in unemployment was noticeably smaller than overall. This could mean that the worst is over in job losses in the manufacturing industry," Jagoda said.
But he added that the construction sector remained very weak in February, and that the economy provided no stimulus for jobs creation.

Separately, the Bundesbank said Thursday it left the German discount and Lombard rates unchanged after a regular meeting of its policy-making council. The German discount rate remains at 2.50 percent and the Lombard emergency financing rate at 4.50 percent.

Economists said the unemployment report would not prompt the Bundesbank to cut rates and said they see no chance of a rate cut any time soon, in part because the real interest rate level is very low and the country's monetary policy was on an expansive course.
Uwe Angenendt of BHF-Bank said the February data confirmed his belief that the rise in unemployment was caused by special factors in January such as cold weather.
But he added that he raised his estimation of Germany's 1997 budget deficit to 3.3 percent of gross domestic product from 3 percent.
High unemployment makes it harder for Germany to cut its budget deficit because it diminishes tax revenue and increases spending for jobless benefits.
Countries hoping to participate in EMU should have budget deficits of 3 percent of GDP or below. The decision on who will participate in EMU at the start will be based on 1997 economic data.
In west Germany, the adjusted number of unemployed fell by 4,000 to 3.018 million in February. The unemployment rate was unchanged at 10.6 percent.
In east Germany, the adjusted number of unemployed rose by 9,000 to 1.298 million. The unemployment rate was 18.9 percent, up from 18.7 percent.
